A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably despite additions and repagination.

before.justification: V1 reports original flow-matching experiments on synthetic transport benchmarks, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-32, and ImageNet-64, including reconstruction, curvature, likelihood, FID, and timing results.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds empirical warm-start and PCA speedup studies in Appendix A.3–A.4.

M1.justification: Section 3 adds cross-batch Sinkhorn warm-starting through extended dual potentials and matching with PCA-projected dot products. These introduce substantive changes to initialization and cost computation, although the flow architectures and training objective remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same two synthetic transport benchmarks and unconditional generation on CIFAR-10, ImageNet-32, and ImageNet-64. The new speedup studies use retained datasets and tasks; PCA changes the matching procedure rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: New Tables 2–3 introduce explicit reference comparisons against Sinkhorn without warm-starting and full-dimensional matching for the added variants. Existing I-FM and ground-truth-pairing comparisons remain unchanged. Newly cited Kim et al. is not added as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols compare warm-start runtime across batch sizes and regularization levels, and test PCA dimensions 500, 1000, 3000, and 12288 at fixed ImageNet-64 batch size 131072 and epsilon 0.1. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, architectures, and training budgets are retained; the PDFs do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3–A.4 adds controlled studies of whether warm-starting reduces computation and whether PCA preserves generation quality while accelerating matching. Tables 2–3 substantially extend the existing batch-size, entropy, and numerical-stability analyses with evidence about two new components.

E5.justification: Table 3 newly discloses that its full-dimensional result uses a different training seed from Table 1. This is additional seed information, not evidence of increased repeated-run counts. No new confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures are reported.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original figures retain their results. New Tables 2–3 add substantial computational-performance evidence: at batch size 524288 and epsilon 0.003, warm-starting takes 4916.29 seconds versus 9207.89 without it. PCA with k=500 takes 1.45 seconds versus 14.1 at full dimension, with four-step FID 48.4 versus 47.3. These are added comparisons, not revisions of v1 scores.

T1.justification: V3 adds Proposition 2's claimed conditional-variance lower bound proportional to n^(-2/r). Appendix A.1 introduces coupling and intrinsic-dimension assumptions, restates the result as Proposition 6, and supplies Lemma 7 and proofs. This is a substantial theoretical addition; the proof's squared-versus-unsquared distance inconsistency limits its validity as written.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims about large, suitably regularized Sinkhorn couplings, normalized entropy, numerical stability, and flow quality. The new methods and theoretical support do not redefine those headline claims.

C2.justification: Section 3 adds an interpretation of batch-size difficulty through intrinsic dimension, including mitigation under the manifold hypothesis. Appendix A.4 explains similar PCA couplings through approximate dot-product preservation. Existing benchmark interpretations and the limitation concerning unablated training hyperparameters remain.

D1.justification: V1 described separating pairing from model training; v3 specifies storing data identifiers with PRNG keys and regenerating paired noise during training. It also documents warm-starting as the default and supplies concrete PCA configurations and runtime measurements, improving practical implementation information.

R1.justification: V3 adds Kim et al.'s Simple Reflow and acknowledges its batch sizes up to 4096 and fixed regularization example. It also contrasts the new lower bound with previously cited minimax results. Other bibliographic changes, including Tong's publication year, concern retained works.

P1.justification: The existing narrative is largely retained, with localized wording edits and inserted method and theory subsections. Appendix sections are renumbered, author order changes, and the internship footnote adds equal-contribution information. There is no extensive rewrite of the existing argument.

P2.justification: V3 adds Tables 2–3 and rearranges existing floats, including placing Figures 11 and 12 together. The original 14 figures retain their graphical content. Table 1 keeps its structure and values while its caption changes from 'Validation FID' to 'FID'.

improvement.justification: The new speedup ablations and reusable-pair implementation details strengthen practical usefulness. However, Appendix A.1 defines D as squared distance in Lemma 7 and then treats it as unsquared distance in the subsequent derivation, leaving the claimed n^(-2/r) variance bound unestablished as written. These practical gains coexist with an unresolved defect in substantial new theoretical support, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
